item.title: How "Certainty" Undermines Intimacy and New Possibilities
item.description:
Relationships

How "Certainty" Undermines Intimacy and New Possibilities

Personal Perspective: A segue to creativity and hope.

Posted August 9, 2026

Key points
  • Certainty limits intimacy and blocks new possibilities in relationships and creativity.
  • Embracing uncertainty fosters deeper empathy, creativity, and meaningful connections.
  • Accepting ambiguity allows for mutual growth and the emergence of unique human potential.

"The only thing that makes life possible is permanent, intolerable uncertainty: not knowing what comes next." –Ursula K Le Guin

"Creative minds exist to disrupt this false peace and force people to face reality" –James Baldwin.

“To be nobody-but-yourself—in a world which is doing its best, night and day, to make you everybody else—means to fight the hardest battle which any human being can fight.” –E.E. Cummings

"Certainty" has been drilled in us as the preferred goal in Western education and industrialism. It permeates our media, politics, and marketing strategies. It is the root cause of those seeking power and the source of unresolved interrelational conflicts. Intimacy is the infinite ways to navigate the complexity of our everyday relationships. It covers the tending to the needs of others through empathy, altruism, and beyond superficial friendships.

Our Lives Can Change By Exploring New Possibilities

How would it be, for instance, if we created a different emphasis in our culture? Nora Bateson poses the question: what if we change "proving to learning from each other"? If we consider this profound change, we are opening the door to infinite contexts that are beyond mere content. It is terrain more than any map of certainty can depict. It encourages novel possibilities of interaction that can bring our hidden needs to the surface and mutually share how our commonalities are also uniquely different, yet worth sharing, as nature does to balance its simultaneous messy and beautiful existence.

Source: NatashaRabin.com, used with permission

If this is experienced in that space between us, those natural pauses that bring up the depth of our humanity, the more our lives will respond differently. Bertrand Russell insisted that the key to a fulfilling life is to “make your interests gradually wider and more impersonal, until bit by bit the walls of the ego recede, and your life becomes increasingly merged in the universal life."

Models and absolute goals cannot attain this blending with others. They impose uniformity at the expense of the many random joys and sorrows that can be taught amongst each other. This avoids rubber-stamping what the correct way to live is, which we now know produces an emotional quilt by not meeting imposed standards. This is prevalent in mandates and how-to books regarding traditional schooling, parenting, grooming, etc.

Thomas Merton believed that spiritual growth and self-actualization require moving past rigid dogmatic formulas to embrace the mystery, vulnerability, and darkness of our relationships. The word "Sfumato," pointed out recently by Maria Popovo in her Marginalian newsletter, is an Italian Renaissance painting technique that blurred the edges of colors and tones so they transition smoothly without harsh lines. This is a great metaphor for breaking the binds that "certainty" and other cause-and-effect pressures produce by making way for our unique contributions to evolve into the infinite emergence of possibilities.

article continues after advertisement

The Process of Creativity Is Our Hope for the Future

Certainty blinds us from seeing how we are all interdependent. It is hard to see how the whole of our complexity is more than what part we play in maintaining our connections to all that occurs in our social/environmental multi-contextual existence. Yet when we step outside of the cultural constraints that maintain this narrow perspective, the intuitive nature of our yearning to create is unstoppable. It is as Michelangelo would describe the dirty slabs of marble that he carted to his studio, saying to those who made fun of him that there is a beautiful statue in here. It is seeing the landscape from a single grain of sand, as William Blake poetically expressed, or Walt Whitman believing that a “leaf of grass is no less than the journey-work of the stars.”

Source: NatashaRabin.com, used with permission

Although accepting certainty indoctrinates us into the temptation of a false sense of security, the outcome produces many stress factors associated with emotional problems that can be resolved through experiencing the creative nuances of life. Rebecca Solnit believes that not depending on prepackaged solutions creates a tolerance towards "...ambiguity and reframing unpredictability as a manageable asset rather than a threat."

This is further underscored by Ursula K Le Guin, who advocated that "uncertainty drives us forward. The unknown, the unforetold, the unproven, that is what life is based on. Ignorance is the ground of thought. Unproof is the ground of action."

Prompts to Encourage Mutual Learning and Understanding the Needs of Others

Have you ever had trouble conforming, and what fears were associated with that pressure?

What does Nora Bateson mean when she says, “What gives her hope is to go where there is none and see the creative process take place”?

What would occur in your life if a difference that made a difference did not have the pressure of certainty?

How would Ursula K Le Guin's quote of "The only thing that makes life possible is permanent, intolerable uncertainty: not knowing what comes next. Create changes in your everyday activities”?

How would your relationships and intimacy be different if you decided not to spend your life demanding clarity from the future?

article continues after advertisement

What are you missing by not understanding what is in between you and another when in relationships?

How would you feel accepting that life has simultaneous contexts and many truths at the same time rather than certainty? Write a short poem to share about how this feeling can become part of your everyday life.

In what ways will you feel different if you go beyond perceiving absolute truths and allow for the infinite possibilities of our human potential to be accepted?

How do you interpret Martin Buber's most famous quote, "All real life is meeting and that most ideas rely on high probability rather than absolute proof "?

In what ways can you describe the many contexts of intimacy?

How can solutions to problems tolerate ambiguity and reframing unpredictability rather than being a threat?

item.title: Can Happiness Be Bad for Your Health?
item.description:
Happiness

Can Happiness Be Bad for Your Health?

You finally got the thing you wanted. So why does part of you feel worse, not better?

Posted August 9, 2026

Key points
  • Positive experiences are not psychologically positive for everyone.
  • Research suggests that good fortune may be associated with poorer health among people with low self-esteem.
  • Experiences that contradict our self-image can themselves become psychologically unsettling.

Imagine something wonderful just happened. You got the job you'd been circling for years. Or the acceptance letter arrived from your dream school.

By any measure, this should be a good day.

And yet, somewhere underneath the relief, there's a discomfort you can't name.

You should be celebrating but you feel a bit bothered.

You wonder: Why has happiness come with a quiet sadness?

When Good Fortune Backfires

In 1989, psychologists Jonathon Brown and Kathleen McGill studied 261 female students in grades 7 through 11.

First, they measured each student's self-esteem. Then they recorded the positive and negative life events each student had experienced over the previous year, along with how often they had been physically sick. Next, they analyzed how these factors were related.

Here is what they found.

The first result is the one you'd predict: students who had experienced more negative events, such as losses and conflicts, got sick more often. Negative life events were associated with poorer health.

Among people with relatively high self-esteem, more positive life events were associated with better health. No surprise there.

Then came the twist.

Among those with low self-esteem, however, the relationship went in the opposite direction: more positive life events were associated with poorer health.

Brown and McGill strengthened the finding in a second study using actual university health-center visits rather than relying only on self-reported illness. The same pattern appeared.

Fifteen years later, Motoko Shimizu and Brett Pelham tested the idea again in 171 college students.

Again, the pattern held. Among people with low in self-esteem, positive life events were associated with poorer health. In other words, for some people, good news seemed to carry a cost.

Why might good events be associated with negative outcomes for some people?

Why Good News Can Feel Wrong

We tend to assume that people simply want positive feedback and want to think well of themselves.

But decades of research on what psychologists call self-verification suggest something more complicated: We also have a surprisingly strong need for the world to fit with how we already see ourselves.

article continues after advertisement

Research by psychologist William Swann and colleagues has shown that people often seek and respond to information that confirms established views of themselves, even when those views are negative.

Psychologist Tory Higgins at Columbia University has shown something related through his work on self-discrepancy: when important parts of how we see ourselves conflict with one another, that gap can lead to real emotional distress.

This does not mean people enjoy criticism or unhappiness. It means that people often strive for consistency.

A predictable self can feel easier to live with than a flattering but unfamiliar one.

So, a positive event may bring pleasure while simultaneously destabilizing the story a person has been using to understand themselves.

If you expect rejection, rejection hurts, but it does not surprise you. If you believe you are undeserving, disappointment confirms the world you already know.

That may also explain why "just let yourself be happy" can be bad advice.

You cannot simply talk yourself out of a psychological pattern that is helping preserve a coherent sense of self.

The Way Out May Run Through Identity

If positive experiences feel unsettling because they conflict with the self, trying harder to enjoy them may not solve the problem.

The deeper task may be revising the identity that makes those experiences feel out of place.

That can begin with noticing the old story.

article continues after advertisement

What do I believe about the kind of person I am?

Self-awareness, and for some people therapy, can create room to examine those assumptions rather than automatically obeying them.

The goal is not to force yourself to feel happy.

It is to gradually build a self-concept capable of accommodating positive experiences.

Eventually, the unfamiliar can become familiar.

The task isn't simply to force yourself to feel differently.

It's to develop a version of yourself in which good things no longer feel psychologically out of place.

item.title: 3 Pleasurable and Powerful Reasons to Send a Handwritten Note
item.description:
Relationships

3 Pleasurable and Powerful Reasons to Send a Handwritten Note

Handwriting fires up neurons, and personal responses can increase wellbeing.

Posted August 9, 2026

Key points
  • The imprimatur of a writer—handwriting, paper, color—engage the senses.
  • In a fast-moving world, taking a pause to write—and on the other end to open, read, and receive—offers gifts.
  • Just one of those gifts seems to be a hit of dopamine.
Source: Diane N. Solomon

My friend Holly says it’s her therapy to handcraft cards. Happy birthday, thinking of you, sending deep sympathy; whatever it is, it’s her meditation and I shamelessly benefit. I buy them by the bundle, and she insists on selling them on the cheap. Then, I have to use them to keep rotating my supply.

Recently, my 94-year-old father, to whom I sent one of Holly's birthday cards, told me it was the most unique birthday card he’d ever received. After 94 years, he’s earned the right to judge. And hyperbole- or exaggeration-prone, my father is not.

Taking the time to send a handwritten card (let alone create one), takes pausing in a nonstop day. Finding or unearthing the right card or paper. Pen, stamp, physical address. Return address, envelope, mailbox. It seems almost… antiquated. Some adults need help: what side does the stamp go on again? How do I write the address? What’s a “return address,” anyway? Luckily, it’s a cinch to consult AI, or even good ‘ol Google. I sound a bit antiquated even to myself, writing about it.

Yet science offers multiple reasons to take the time and space to reach out—in handwriting. For starters:

  • Handwriting engages more brain circuits than typing. This makes sense: using your hand in the swirling motions of writing, engaging fine motor skills, creating all those different letter shapes… compared to the repetitive tap-tap-tapping on key after key. Typing definitely has benefits in speed and ease. But handwriting engages sensory, motor, and cognitive processes across more brain regions, according to neural imaging. It even improves memory and learning (a good endorsement for handwritten notetaking). Typing, while critical, engages less neural circuitry and is simply more passive, physically and cognitively. Who doesn’t aspire to more cognitive connections and “muscle”?
  • Snail mail offers dopamine. Subscribing to clubs that send curated cards, papers, stickers, postcards, stationery supplies, etc., is super trendy right now. Perhaps begun by people in recovery to boost dopamine they might be missing from harmful substances of choice, the analog movement has taken this big time. People yearn to slow down, use their hands for something positive and meditative. While any art or craft—from needlepoint to scrapbooking to woodworking to painting—may do, a handwritten note or card can be written on a coffee break and offers quick satisfaction and accomplishment. You’re reaching out to tell someone you’re thinking of them, you love them, they matter to you. The old adage that it’s better to give than to receive is born out in research, too: You’re giving a mini-treasured-gift with a card, note, or letter—and you’re getting at least as many good feelings in return.
  • Sending snail mail shows responsiveness, a critical action in healthy relationships. Think about it: You haven’t heard from someone in a while. They’re probably busy, you tell yourself, but perhaps you worry: Did that loving comment I made about their “new, '90s” hairdo land wrong? Are they mad I forgot to follow up when they said they were having a hard day? Do they have cooler friends now, much cooler than I am? Then, you receive a postcard in the mail. All that worry? Hogwash. They love you, they were just busy, and the card reinforces it. Responsiveness to (and from) others fosters growth and wellbeing, individually and in relationships. Sure, a text can do in a pinch, but a postcard you set on the counter? Every time you saunter into the kitchen and see it, you re-feel that ping of love, silently sending love (or care, safety, support, and so on), back. Improved health and wellbeing packaged up tiny, in a note.
article continues after advertisement

Sending snail mail takes a small effort of time and energy that reaps great benefits. It gives pause and rest, time to slow down; thinking of someone you care about and letting them know it, too. This feels lovely both ways—and even more so because of what a rare touch it is in today’s world. I’d say even more, but I have a friend I’ve been meaning to write….

Source: Diane N. Solomon
